answers.primary: Permission deny rules placed in managed settings: Read(secrets/**) and Edit(secrets/**) plus Bash deny rules for the commands that touch that path, locked down with allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly so user and project settings cannot add competing rules. Because Read and Edit deny rules do not cover arbitrary subprocesses that open files themselves, pair them with sandboxing, whose filesystem boundary is merged from sandbox.filesystem settings and the Read/Edit deny rules, for OS-level enforcement over Bash and its children.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook that inspects each call and exits 2. It is also harness-run, but the docs are explicit that the permission system, not a hook, is the way to enforce a hard allow or deny, and a hook that has to parse arbitrary shell text is best-effort where a deny rule is evaluated first and unconditionally.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Deny rules are evaluated before allow rules and before any hook decision, from any scope, and a managed-settings deny cannot be overridden by project settings, user settings, --allowedTools, or a PreToolUse hook returning allow. Nothing about the outcome depends on the model agreeing.
answers.context_boundary: The rules live in settings files that never enter the model's context window; the model only sees the refusal when a blocked call returns an error. A bare tool-name deny goes further and removes the tool from Claude's context entirely, so the capability is not visible to be argued about.
answers.lifecycle: Loaded at settings resolution on session start and applied on every tool call for the life of the session, in every mode including bypassPermissions for the sandbox layer. It stops applying only when the rule is edited out of the managed settings file or the policy chain stops being read; a crafted prompt cannot suspend it mid-session.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed at the built-in tool layer, but has a documented gap: Read and Edit deny rules cover Claude's file tools and the Bash file commands Claude Code recognises (cat, head, tail, sed) and not a python or node script that opens the file itself, so without the sandbox a shell command can still reach secrets/. The other practical failure is silent: a rule written as Write(secrets/**) or NotebookEdit(secrets/**) is accepted but never consulted by file permission checks, so compliance thinks it is covered while only a startup warning says otherwise.
answers.version_caveat: A Read deny rule also blocking the Edit tool on the same path requires v2.1.208 or later, and the rule-shape restriction (only Edit(path) and Read(path) are consulted, with a startup warning for Write/NotebookEdit/MultiEdit/Glob path rules) requires v2.1.210 or later; write Edit(secrets/**) rather than Write(secrets/**). allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly and the sandbox allowManagedReadPathsOnly key are read only from managed settings, so they need the enterprise managed-settings deployment path, and on Windows paths normalise to POSIX form (//c/**) before matching.

answers.primary: A skill: .claude/skills/release/SKILL.md holding a short ordered spine, with the bulk of the 400 lines split into supporting reference files the skill links to and loads only when needed, and the two helper scripts left as executables the skill tells Claude to run (referenced through ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}) so their bodies never enter context at all. Only the skill's name and description are resident in an unrelated conversation; the full body loads on /release or when Claude matches the description.
answers.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md (or a .claude/rules/ file). Both load their full content at session start and are re-billed on every request, which is exactly the recurring cost the team is objecting to.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness guarantees only that the description is listed and that the rendered body is injected once the skill is invoked; whether Claude follows the 400 lines in order, and whether it picks the skill up at all when nobody types the command, is a model decision.
answers.context_boundary: Runs inline in the main session context. What crosses is the description (always, capped at 1,536 characters combined with when_to_use) and then the rendered SKILL.md as a single message on invocation; supporting reference files cross only when Claude reads them, and script bodies never cross because they are executed rather than loaded.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered by /release or by Claude matching the description to the task. Once invoked, the content stays in the conversation for the rest of the session and is not re-read on later turns, so it stops applying only when the session ends; after auto-compaction the most recent invocation is re-attached at up to 5,000 tokens within a 25,000-token shared budget.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory. The two realistic failures are non-triggering (a vague description means Claude never loads it during the weekly release and the team is back to pasting) and the inverse, that once loaded on release day the whole body is resident for every subsequent turn of that session, so the saving is across sessions rather than within one. Write the body as standing instructions rather than one-time steps, because Claude Code does not re-read the file mid-session.
answers.version_caveat: No plan gate or experimental flag. Re-invocation deduplication (a note instead of a second full copy) requires v2.1.202 or later; before that every re-invocation appended another copy, which reintroduces the cost complaint. ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR} substitution inside allowed-tools requires v2.1.129 or later and ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} requires v2.1.196, otherwise the helper-script rules stay literal and prompt. Adding disable-model-invocation: true drops the description cost to zero but gives up automatic loading.

answers.primary: An MCP server for the tracker, added as a remote HTTP server (claude mcp add --transport http tracker <url>) at project scope so the .mcp.json is checked in and the whole team gets the same tools, with authentication handled by the server's OAuth 2.0 flow completed once from /mcp or claude mcp login. Claude then reads and updates tickets through purpose-built tools instead of prose pasted into chat.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill that scripts curl calls against the tracker's REST API. It can carry the endpoint knowledge but has nowhere to hold an OAuth session, so it would push a bearer token into a file or an env var and re-implement refresh; MCP owns connection and auth, and a skill is the right layer only for teaching Claude the team's ticket conventions on top of it.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the connection, the OAuth token storage and the automatic refresh-and-retry on 401, and it owns permission prompts for the tools. The model owns the outcome that matters here, which is choosing to call the tracker tools rather than asking a human to paste ticket text.
answers.context_boundary: The server's tool names load into the main session context at startup with full schemas deferred until a tool is used; ticket bodies and update results cross into the main window as tool results, one call at a time, instead of arriving as a pasted wall of text. With tool search enabled, tool definitions are fetched on demand rather than all being resident.
answers.lifecycle: Connects at session start and reconnects automatically; the OAuth token refreshes silently and the server is flagged in /mcp only when a refresh also fails. It stops applying when the server is disabled or removed, when Clear authentication is used, or when a higher-precedence definition of the same name (local scope beats project beats user) shadows it.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed and visibly: an expired or rejected refresh token means the tools are simply unavailable and Claude Code shows a startup notice pointing at /mcp, so the worst case is the team falling back to pasting, which is the outcome they were trying to eliminate. The sharp edge is non-interactive use: there is no /mcp panel in claude -p or the Agent SDK, so the OAuth flow cannot run there and someone must sign in from an interactive session first. A configured headers.Authorization that the server rejects reports a failed connection rather than falling back to OAuth.
answers.version_caveat: No plan restriction. claude mcp login for signing in from the shell requires v2.1.186 or later, and its no-local-browser detection and --no-browser flag require v2.1.191; the reliable-refresh behaviour (a transient refresh failure no longer flags the server for the whole session) requires v2.1.206, and the startup notice v2.1.193. Project-scoped .mcp.json servers prompt for approval before first use, resettable with claude mcp reset-project-choices. A self-hosted server with a pre-registered redirect URI needs --callback-port, and restricted scopes may need --client-id with pre-configured credentials.

answers.primary: A SessionStart hook registered in the repository's .claude/settings.json, matching startup (and resume, clear, compact, fork if the context should be refreshed on those too), running a fast script that queries the sprint tooling and git and returns the result either as plain stdout or as hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext. That text is placed in Claude's context before the first prompt, so the session opens already knowing the ticket list and branch.
answers.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md. It is the documented choice for static per-project context, but it is a checked-in file, so it cannot pull the sprint list and the current branch live at the moment the session opens; it would go stale between sprints and every session would pay for the stale copy.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook fires deterministically on the lifecycle event with no model involvement and no one needing to ask. The model owns only what it does with the injected text afterwards.
answers.context_boundary: The script runs in its own process with no context window of its own; only its stdout or additionalContext crosses into the main session context, once, before the first user turn. Keep the payload tight, because whatever crosses is resident for the rest of the session and is re-billed every request.
answers.lifecycle: Fires at session begin and again on resume, clear, compaction and fork according to the matcher, and is done once its output is injected; the text is a snapshot that does not refresh itself mid-session. Claude Code saves the injected text in the transcript, and SessionStart hooks re-run on resume with source set to resume or fork so they can produce fresh values rather than replaying stale ones.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open. If the script errors, times out, or the tracker is unreachable, the stderr is shown to the user only, exit code 2 does not block, and the session starts anyway with no sprint context and possibly nobody noticing. The other practical problem is latency: this runs on every session, so a slow tracker call delays every launch. If you implement the lookup as an mcp_tool hook, expect a not-connected error on first run because SessionStart typically fires before MCP servers finish connecting; a command hook that shells out is safer.
answers.version_caveat: No plan gate. Only command and mcp_tool hook types are supported on SessionStart (no http, prompt, or agent hooks). Forked sessions report source fork only from v2.1.214; earlier versions report resume. The companion fields are version-sensitive too: reloadSkills matters only if the hook installs skills, initialUserMessage applies in -p mode, and exit-code-2 stderr has rendered in the transcript only since v2.1.199.

answers.primary: A plugin, distributed through a private plugin marketplace the platform team owns. Package the review helper as skills/ (namespaced, /platform:code-review), the lifecycle automations as hooks/hooks.json, and the tracker integration as the plugin's .mcp.json, with an explicit version field in .claude-plugin/plugin.json so consumers only take updates when the team bumps it. Each of the 40 repos opts in through enabledPlugins and extraKnownMarketplaces in its .claude/settings.json, or the org force-enables the plugin in managed settings.
answers.rejected_alternative: Standalone .claude/ configuration copied into each repository. It works for one project, but there is no version, no update channel and no single place to fix a bug, so 40 copies drift apart the first time the review helper changes.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns loading, namespacing and version resolution, and managed settings can force-enable the plugin so a repo cannot silently drop it. The model owns whether the skills actually get used once loaded; the hooks inside the plugin are the harness-owned part of the bundle.
answers.context_boundary: Everything loads into whichever session enables the plugin: skill descriptions and subagent definitions occupy main-session context, MCP tool names load at startup with schemas on demand, and hooks cost nothing until they return output. Nothing crosses between the 40 consuming repos; the plugin is the shared artifact, not shared state.
answers.lifecycle: Applies from the moment the plugin is enabled in a repo and reloads on /reload-plugins within a session. Updates reach consumers when the marketplace entry moves and the consumer updates: with an explicit version, only a bump ships an update; without one, a git-distributed plugin treats every commit as a new version. It stops applying on disable or uninstall, or when a --plugin-dir local copy shadows it for a session.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory at the distribution layer unless you force it. Repos that never run the update, or that pin an old marketplace commit, quietly keep the old helper, so 'reaches every consumer' is only true if managed settings force-enable the plugin or strictPluginOnlyCustomization is set. Structural mistakes are the other common failure: putting skills/, hooks/ or agents/ inside .claude-plugin/ instead of at the plugin root makes components silently not load, and a same-named project or user agent overrides the plugin's.
answers.version_caveat: No plan gate for authoring or private distribution. Version behaviour hinges on the optional version field (omit it and every commit SHA counts as a new version). Keeping the marketplace in a private repository is the supported way to stay internal; the public community marketplace requires review and, for the claude.ai submission form, a Team or Enterprise org. Managed-settings levers (enabledPlugins force-enable, allowManagedHooksOnly, strictPluginOnlyCustomization) are read only from managed settings, and --plugin-dir cannot override a plugin that managed settings force-enable or force-disable.

answers.primary: A skill for the deploy procedure with disable-model-invocation: true in its frontmatter, so it is invocable only by a human typing /deploy and is not even visible to Claude as an option. Add allowed-tools scoped to the exact deploy commands so the run does not stall on prompts, and consider context: fork if the procedure's output should not flood the main conversation. This is the documented pattern for workflows with side effects, precisely so Claude cannot decide to deploy because the code looks ready.
answers.rejected_alternative: A CLAUDE.md rule saying 'never deploy unless the user asks'. That is a request the model interprets, not a gate; the whole point of the requirement is that it must hold even when the model's own reasoning concludes the code is ready.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness for the trigger: with disable-model-invocation set, Claude Code does not put the skill in Claude's context and does not let the model load it, so the invocation gate does not depend on model restraint. The model still owns execution quality once a human types the command.
answers.context_boundary: Main session context, and nothing at all until the human types the command: the description is withheld, so the skill has zero context cost while unused. On invocation the rendered body enters as one message and stays for the session. With context: fork the procedure runs in a subagent's own window and only its result returns.
answers.lifecycle: Starts only on the explicit /deploy invocation (and, from v2.1.196, is likewise blocked from firing when a scheduled task names the skill as its prompt). The allowed-tools grant covers just that turn and clears at your next message; the instructions themselves persist in context for the session.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for the skill, but open for the underlying capability: the flag stops Claude from invoking the deploy skill, not from running the deploy commands directly if it decides to. If the guarantee has to be absolute, back it with a permission deny rule (or a PreToolUse hook) on the deploy command itself and let the skill be the human-triggered path through that gate. The secondary cost is that Claude cannot suggest the skill either, since it is invisible until invoked.
answers.version_caveat: No plan restriction. disable-model-invocation defaults to false, so the gate exists only if you set it; from v2.1.218 it accepts yes/on/1 as well as true. Its coverage of scheduled tasks requires v2.1.196 or later, and it also prevents the skill from being preloaded into subagents. The background: false option for a forked skill requires v2.1.218.

answers.primary: A GitHub Action in the repository's workflow config, triggered on the issues opened event, running Claude Code non-interactively in the CI runner with a prompt that labels the issue, searches open issues for likely duplicates, and posts the first-response comment through the GitHub API with a scoped token. GitHub Actions is the documented option for tasks tied to repo events that should live alongside the workflow config, and it is the only one of the options that needs no machine of yours to be awake.
answers.rejected_alternative: A Routine (an Anthropic-managed scheduled or event-triggered run configured at claude.ai/code/routines). It can also fire on GitHub events without a terminal, but the triage logic should be versioned and reviewed in the same repository as the workflow it serves, and it needs the runner's checkout and repo credentials.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness, in the sense that the CI system owns the trigger and the run: the webhook fires the job whether or not any model judges the issue interesting. The content of the triage (which label, which duplicate, what the comment says) is model-owned and unreviewed, which is the part with no guarantee attached.
answers.context_boundary: An ephemeral context per issue, inside the runner. The issue title and body and whatever duplicate search results the job gathers cross in; labels and a comment cross out to GitHub. Nothing carries over to the next issue or into any developer's local session, so give the job everything it needs in the prompt.
answers.lifecycle: Starts on the issues opened webhook and ends when the job exits; there is no session to resume and no state between runs. It stops applying when the workflow file is removed or disabled, or when the event filter no longer matches.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open: if the job errors, the API rate-limits, or the token lacks the scope, the issue is simply left untriaged and nobody at a terminal notices. The more expensive failure is silent wrongness, since a mislabel or a confidently wrong duplicate claim is posted publicly with no human in the loop; keep the token least-privilege, make the first-response comment hedged, and prefer suggesting a duplicate over closing one.
answers.version_caveat: I cannot state the action's version, plan, or authentication requirements from my permitted inputs: the documentation mirror I have does not include the GitHub Actions page, only a pointer to it from the scheduling comparison. One caveat I can state from the mirror: as of v2.1.210 the ultracode keyword does not start a dynamic workflow when it arrives via a webhook payload or a pull request comment relayed into the conversation, or via a -p prompt, so untrusted issue text cannot escalate the run that way; before v2.1.210 it could.

answers.primary: An agent team: the session becomes the lead and spawns five teammates, one per hypothesis, instructed to message each other directly and try to disprove each other's theories, with the shared task list coordinating and a findings document as the written deliverable. This is the documented use case for debugging with competing hypotheses, and the adversarial debate is the mechanism, since it is what defeats the anchoring a single investigator falls into.
answers.rejected_alternative: Subagents. They parallelise just as well, but they can only report back to the main agent and never talk to each other, so there is no direct back-and-forth and the lead would have to relay every challenge, which reintroduces the single point of anchoring.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness provides the mailboxes, the task list with file-locked claiming, and the spawn mechanics, but which hypothesis survives, when the debate is over, and what the consensus says are all model judgements. Hooks (TeammateIdle, TaskCompleted) are the only place to put a harness-owned gate on that.
answers.context_boundary: Six context windows: the lead's plus one per teammate, each fully independent. Each teammate loads project CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills itself but does not inherit the lead's conversation history, so the spawn prompt must carry the bug details. What crosses between them is SendMessage traffic through the JSON mailboxes, the shared task list, and files written to disk, which is why the consensus should land in a document rather than only in someone's window.
answers.lifecycle: The team forms when the first teammate spawns and is scoped to that session; the lead is fixed for the session's lifetime and teammates cannot spawn their own. It ends when teammates are asked to shut down or the session exits, at which point the team config directory is cleaned up automatically while the task list persists under cleanupPeriodDays retention.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory, expensive, and prone to stalling. Token cost scales linearly with five separate Claude instances; teammates sometimes stop on errors rather than recovering, task status lags so dependent work blocks, and the lead may declare the investigation finished before the debate has converged (tell it to wait). Two teammates editing the same findings file overwrite each other, so give the write to one owner. Nothing in the mechanism guarantees the surviving theory is correct; it is a bias-reduction pattern, not a proof.
answers.version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default: nothing happens without CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 in settings.json or the environment. The no-setup-step spawn and automatic cleanup describe v2.1.178 and later (TeamCreate and TeamDelete no longer exist, and team_name is accepted but ignored). Known limits: /resume and /rewind do not restore in-process teammates, one team per session, no nested teams, and split panes need tmux or iTerm2 with it2, which rules them out in VS Code's terminal, Windows Terminal and Ghostty.

answers.primary: A custom output style: a Markdown file in the project's .claude/output-styles/ defining the data-analyst role and the fixed tabular report format, with keep-coding-instructions left out (it defaults to false) so Claude Code's built-in software-engineering instructions are dropped rather than appended to. Select it for everyone by setting outputStyle in the checked-in .claude/settings.json rather than relying on each person's /config choice, which is saved to their own settings.local.json.
answers.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md. It adds a user message after the system prompt and cannot remove the default engineering instructions, so the analyst persona would be competing with the coding system prompt every turn instead of replacing it.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the injection (the style's text is appended to the system prompt, the built-in coding instructions are omitted, and reminders to adhere to the style are issued during the conversation). The model owns adherence to the tabular format on any given turn, which is where this stops being a guarantee.
answers.context_boundary: The main conversation's system prompt only. Subagents run their own system prompt and are unaffected, so any work routed through a subagent comes back without the analyst framing; a fork is the exception, since it inherits the parent's full system prompt. The added instructions raise input tokens, mitigated by prompt caching after the first request.
answers.lifecycle: Read once at session start, then applies to every turn of that session. Changing or switching the style takes effect only after /clear or a new session, and switching it invalidates the prompt cache. It stops applying when outputStyle is changed back or the session ends.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory. The style shapes the system prompt but does not validate output, so Claude can drift out of the table format on a long or unusual turn, and there is no hook-free way to catch that; if the format is contractual, add a Stop or PostToolUse check. Two quieter failures: dropping the coding instructions also drops the built-in guidance on scoping changes and verifying work, which matters if the annotation project ever touches code; and a teammate who edited the style mid-session sees no change until /clear.
answers.version_caveat: No plan restriction. The standalone /output-style command was deprecated in v2.1.73 and removed in v2.1.91, so drive it from /config or the outputStyle setting. Nested project output-style directories resolve closest-to-working-directory from v2.1.178. If you later ship the style in a plugin, force-for-plugin applies it automatically and overrides the user's outputStyle setting, with the first loaded plugin winning when several set it.

answers.primary: A non-interactive headless invocation (claude -p, or the Agent SDK wrapping it) from the existing CI job, with the environment pinned by flags rather than by whatever is on the runner: --strict-mcp-config passed without --mcp-config so no MCP servers load at all, --setting-sources restricted to project (or --settings pointing at a checked-in JSON file), and --bare or --safe-mode to skip auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins and CLAUDE.md. Add --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections so per-machine details (working directory, environment info, memory paths) move out of the system prompt, and --output-format json or --json-schema so the job parses a fixed shape.
answers.rejected_alternative: Shipping the typo-and-lint pass as a project skill or plugin checked into the repo. It makes the instructions shared and versioned, but it does nothing about isolation: the run would still load the runner user's settings, hooks and .mcp.json alongside it, which is exactly the leakage being ruled out.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness, for the part that can be owned: the CLI flags decide deterministically what configuration is discovered and loaded, and no model decision affects that. Nobody owns byte-for-byte output equality, which is the part of the requirement that is not a configuration property.
answers.context_boundary: One ephemeral headless context per pull request, inside the CI runner. The diff goes in as the prompt and the review comes out on stdout; with the isolation flags set, no user-level CLAUDE.md, hook output, skill description or MCP tool definition crosses into that window. Pair with --no-session-persistence so the run leaves nothing on disk to be resumed or reused.
answers.lifecycle: Starts when the CI job invokes the command for a given diff and ends when the process exits; there is no session state, no resume, and nothing carried to the next pull request. It stops applying the moment the workflow stops passing the flags, which is why they belong in the checked-in workflow file rather than a developer's shell.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open in the direction that matters: forget --strict-mcp-config and the project's .mcp.json joins the run silently, and forget the setting-source restriction and a teammate's user-level hooks fire without any error to signal it, so the run still succeeds and just is not the run you specified. And the stated requirement is not fully achievable: these flags remove configuration variance, not model variance, so identical inputs can still produce different words. If byte-identical output is a hard requirement, the deterministic part has to be a linter and the model output has to be treated as advisory commentary.
answers.version_caveat: No plan gate. --safe-mode requires v2.1.169 or later and, importantly, still applies managed settings policy including policy-configured hooks, status line and file-suggestion commands, so it is not total isolation on a managed machine; --bare differs by also relaxing permissions handling. --json-schema errors on an invalid schema only from v2.1.205 (before that it silently produced unstructured output), and --append-subagent-system-prompt requires v2.1.205. --tools does not affect MCP tools, so rely on --strict-mcp-config rather than a tool list to keep MCP out.
